name: Prostanozol

lead: Prostanozol is a designer oral steroid sold in bodybuilding supplements from around 2005, aimed at a stanozolol-like effect of lean muscle and a drier look. It is a prodrug of a stanozolol analogue that lacks the 17-alpha-methyl group.

In the body it is described as converting to that analogue, which acts as an androgen receptor agonist. It has no clinical trials; published work covers doping-detection metabolism, supplement-contamination surveys and legal classification.

paras: It was sold as an oral dietary-supplement ingredient. In 2012 the US DEA classified it, with methasterone, as a Schedule III anabolic steroid.
Human safety has not been studied. It is a US Schedule III substance and prohibited in sport; a 2007 marathon runner received a two-year ban after testing positive for it and testosterone.

angle.text: A designer prohormone sold in supplements that converts in the body to a stanozolol-like steroid acting on the androgen receptor, for lean muscle and a drier look. It is now Schedule III in the US and has no clinical data.

lead: Prostanozol, also called demethylstanozolol tetrahydropyran ether, is a designer anabolic-androgenic steroid that acts as a prodrug of the 17α-demethylated analogue of stanozolol (Winstrol) [1]. It is taken by mouth [1].

It was first identified in 2005 as an ingredient in products sold as bodybuilding "dietary supplements" [1]. In 2007 Russian marathon runner Lyubov Denisova tested positive for prostanozol and testosterone and received a two-year ban [1]. In 2012 the US Drug Enforcement Administration classified it, along with methasterone, as a Schedule III anabolic steroid [2].
Published work is limited to doping-control metabolism studies and supplement-contamination surveys; there are no clinical trials [3][4].

paras: Prostanozol appeared in 2005 in supplements marketed to bodybuilders [1]. The 2007 Denisova case is among its best-known doping findings [1]. A 2008 review of nutritional supplements found that many were contaminated with, or faked with, doping substances, illustrating the wider context in which such products circulated [3]. Wikipedia describes it as one of the substances banned by the International Olympic Committee and as prohibited by WADA [1].

It is described as a prodrug that is converted into a stanozolol-like steroid lacking the 17α-methyl group [1]. A 2016 study used humanised chimeric mice and human liver microsomes to map its metabolism, motivated by the fact that ethical limits prevent excretion studies in volunteers for designer steroids [4].
A 2012 DEA final rule classified prostanozol (17β-hydroxy-5α-androstano[3,2-c]pyrazole) and methasterone as Schedule III anabolic steroids under the Controlled Substances Act [2].
No studies found in humans. Related research consists of metabolism work in mice and liver microsomes [4] and surveys of supplement contamination [3].
